newsitem.title: USA: Dollar recovers from overseas lows to close mixed.
newsitem.headline: Dollar recovers from overseas lows to close mixed.

text.p: The dollar recovered from early overseas losses Friday to close mixed against other major currencies, traders said.
The dollar was forced below critical support levels at 1.5050 marks and 110.80 yen in Asian and European trading before a significant number of buyers were enticed.

"The sell-off bottomed right at the New York opening as we saw some very good buying interest under 110.70 yen and 1.5050 marks," said Ben Strauss, associate vice-president at Bank Julius Baer and Co.
The dollar closed almost unchanged at 1.5093 marks, versus 1.5090 marks at Thursday's close. Against the yen, the dollar finished lower at 111.07 yen from 111.43 yen.
Many traders were caught ill-positioned, having bought yen and sold Swiss francs and marks, when the dollar moved higher against the yen.
Dealers scrambled to sell yen to cover outstanding positions, which aided the dollar, other dealers said.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's affirmation late Thursday of his longstanding strong-dollar policy also helped to stop the dollar's slide overseas, they said.

"Without a change in Rubin's strong-dollar stance, it's hard to warrant really pushing the move a lot lower, especially with the 110 dollar/yen psychological level being so close," said Seth Garrett, chief dealer at CS First Boston.
The dollar rose after hitting a fresh 49-month low against the British pound of $1.6680 in overseas trade to close little changed at $1.6635 from Thursday's close of $1.6645.
Dealers sold pounds for dollars to lock in profits earned from the pound's recent meteoric rise against both the dollar and the mark.

Strong recent British economic data that suggest higher interest rates in the near future have fuelled the sharp gains in sterling. Rising British rates would increase returns on investments in pound-denominated assets.

Dealers sold Swiss francs, mostly against the yen, after the Swiss government said its pension funds, with invested assets estimated at close to 30 billion Swiss francs, may now place some of their holdings in bonds denominated in foreign currencies.
"There is some concern over increased capital outflows out of Switzerland, which is more bearish news for the Swiss franc," Strauss said.
"To add to the flames, mark/Swiss franc has been moving steadily higher for several weeks and that has increased the pressure on the Swiss franc."
The dollar closed at 1.2792 Swiss francs, up from 1.2757 at Thursday's close.
In other trading, the dollar ended at Canadian $1.3388, up from C$1.3356 on late Thursday.
